hints.junior: That one-line embed script gets the same DOM and cookie access as your own code — an AI widget that scrapes page text for 'context' scrapes whatever's actually on the page.
hints.mid: No browser-level distinction between 'your script' and 'their script' once both share the origin — cookies, DOM, storage, all reachable, all by default.
hints.staff: The failure is silent by design — nothing signals a third party just read your cookies and posted DOM text out, you only catch it by reading its actual network requests.

hints.junior: Click 'Load AI widget' in each mode and watch the log show exactly what the widget could read and what it sent.
hints.mid: Direct script tag mode reads the mock page text plus a mock cookie; sandboxed mode only ever sees the two fields explicitly passed in.
hints.staff: No real network call happens here — this simulates the mechanism locally so you can see what a real integration either way would actually transmit.

hints.junior: Three layers: CSP limits where any script can send data, a sandboxed iframe stops the widget reading your page at all, and an allowlist limits what you hand it in the first place.
hints.mid: sandbox="allow-scripts" with no allow-same-origin puts the widget in an opaque origin — its document.cookie is empty and window.parent throws, it only gets what you postMessage to it.
hints.staff: The allowlist step is independent of sandboxing — even a perfectly sandboxed widget gets over-shared if your integration code serializes a whole user object instead of the two fields the flow needs.

hints.junior: Check what other domains the widget's own script calls — some pull in their own analytics or trackers beyond the vendor you actually chose.
hints.mid: Verify by reading real payloads in DevTools Network, filtered to the widget's domain — no console errors isn't proof the sandbox worked, an actual look at the request body is.
hints.staff: SRI pinning is often impractical for frequently-updated widget bundles — a versioned URL instead of a 'latest' alias is the realistic middle ground, plus check the vendor's terms for whether page context is used for model training by default.

sections.junior: Today's case is about third-party AI chat widgets, and how a single script tag can end up reading way more of your page than you'd expect, including things like internal notes or account details sitting right there in the DOM.
sections.mid: There's no browser-level distinction between your script and a third party's once both are loaded into the same page — a widget's script tag gets full document access by default, with no origin restriction at all.
sections.staff: This isn't a vendor being malicious, it's the default trust model of the same-origin script tag being a poor fit for third-party code with its own incentive to collect data — and the failure mode is silent.

sections.junior: The fix has three parts: a content security policy that limits where scripts can send data, a sandboxed iframe so the widget can't read your page's cookies or content directly, and passing it only the specific fields it actually needs instead of letting it read everything.
sections.mid: A sandboxed iframe with no allow-same-origin puts the widget in a unique, opaque origin — it can't read anything from your page except what you explicitly hand it via postMessage.
sections.staff: The allowlist step matters independently of sandboxing — even a perfectly sandboxed widget can still be handed too much if your integration code passes a whole user object instead of the two fields the flow needs.

sections.junior: Try loading the widget in each mode and watch the log to see exactly what it can read and what it ends up sending out.
sections.mid: In direct script tag mode, the simulated widget reads the mock page's visible text and session cookie and posts both out. In sandboxed plus allowlist mode, it only receives the two fields explicitly passed to it.
sections.staff: This simulates the mechanism without a real network call or vendor — the log shows what a real widget integrated either way would actually be able to observe and transmit.

sections.junior: A widget script tag has the same access as your own code by default. Sandbox it, restrict where it can send data, and only hand it the fields it actually needs.
sections.mid: CSP limits where any script can send data, a sandboxed iframe stops the widget reading your page's DOM and cookies at all, and an explicit field allowlist stops your own code from handing it more than it needs.
sections.staff: Verify the fix by reading actual network payloads in DevTools rather than trusting the absence of console errors.
